idiom_name: plain class over a Hash standing in for the collaborator
implementation_notes: In Ruby the fake is an ordinary object holding a Hash: define the same methods the collaborator exposes and let them read and write the Hash, which gives the working behaviour a fake needs without any interface declaration or framework. RSpec's verifying doubles (instance_double) and stubs are for canned answers and interaction assertions, so they cover the stub and mock rows rather than this one. Build the fake per example, or clear the Hash in a before hook, and keep at least one test against the real collaborator.
code_sketch:
class InMemoryUserRepository
  def initialize
    @users = {}
  end
  def save(user) = @users[user.id] = user
  def find(id) = @users[id]
end
session = Session.new(InMemoryUserRepository.new)
pitfalls: A class variable (@@users) or a constant-backed Hash is shared across examples and leaks state - keep the store in an instance variable.
Hash returns nil for a missing key, so a fake that should raise (or return a result object) rewrites the caller's error path - mirror the real contract.
Duck typing means a typo in a method name only fails when the code under test calls it; instance_double(RealRepository) verifies the fake's interface against the real class.
